If you value this work, undated portrait of Michael Dodd, assistant secretary of war for critical technologies. Photo by the War Department. A senior War Department official who pledged to sell his stake in his family's defense consulting firm still owns between $1 million and $5 million in the company over a year after his confirmation, according to his financial disclosures. The official, Michael Dodd, is the assistant secretary of war for critical technologies. His office writes the Pentagon's technology roadmaps, which lay out what technologies the military needs as well as plans and funding strategies to develop them. In a September 2026 , he said these responsibilities give him "significant influence on what the services procure." The firm he founded, Dioltas, move "critical technology" through the Pentagon contracting process, "from first relationship to strategic partnership to funding." Dodd's wife, Melanie, was the registered agent and treasurer for Dioltas until November, and their son Keegan is its manager, according to government filings. The three of them are listed as the owners of Dioltas's office in Indiana, according to property records. (Their other son, Carson, works as a business analyst at the firm.) Companies listed as Dioltas clients, according to his 2025 nominee report, have won Pentagon contracts or other funding worth up to $4.3 billion since September 2025, more than $100 million of it already committed. Most of that money, up to about $3.5 billion of it, was awarded to Dioltas's clients in contracts that the Pentagon solicited after Dodd was confirmed by the Senate that month. These clients include defense-technology firms ManTech International and JRC Integrated Systems, counter-drone company Allen Control Systems, and the microelectronics manufacturer SkyWater Technology. Drop Site News asked the firms if they were current clients of Dioltas, and whether Dioltas helped them win the Pentagon contracts awarded after Dodd's confirmation. None of the firms responded. Dodd himself did not respond to requests for comment. The full list of Dioltas's current clients is not public. Dodd is one of many federal with ties to and who have assumed in the second Trump administration, as the department steers billions of dollars to new tech firms through fast-tracked contracts, often with limited oversight. Dodd's apparent conflicts of interest are not exceptional. They reflect business as usual under President Donald Trump. From the on down, administration officials have regularly engaged in various forms of self-dealing. President Trump's second term is unique, according to many ethics experts, in its numerous officials' disregard for the separation between public duties and private interests. Dodd worked as an advisor to "several prominent" venture capital funds with defense portfolios, according to his , and shepherded their companies through the Pentagon's acquisition process. He listed 8VC, a , as his sole business relationship aside from Dioltas in his 2025 Senate Armed Services Committee questionnaire. His shows that he began advising the firm in November 2024, but this work is not listed on his 2025 ethics disclosure. It is unclear when Dodd stopped advising 8VC. Between November 2024 and Dodd's March 2025 nomination, 8VC portfolio firms received at least $100 million through deals with the Defense Innovation Unit, a Pentagon initiative with headquarters in Silicon Valley. The unit focuses on forging closer ties between the military and tech industry. At the same time that Dodd was advising 8VC, he held a senior position at the Defense Innovation Unit, where he developed its investment strategy and helped manage funding projects with defense-tech startups, according to his . The Defense Innovation Unit did not respond to Drop Site's questions about Dodd's role with 8VC. 8VC's founder and managing partner is Joe Lonsdale, a Palantir co-founder who is now helping shape the Pentagon's future tech priorities as a in Project Meridian, a that enlists defense-tech investors to advise the future of U.S. warfare. 8VC is a top investor in autonomous military tech firms Anduril--whose founder Palmer Luckey is Meridian's co-director--and Saronic, whose CEO Dino Mavrookas and Gen. James Rainey are also Meridian panelists. Lonsdale has that new defense tech firms "need allies in government," and a nonprofit he controls has the Pentagon on defense contracting reform. 8VC's portfolio firms have done business in Dodd's . For example, Lonsdale co-founded Epirus, a defense contractor that creates directed-energy systems which has received around $30 million since Dodd took office. In September, Dodd said he would "" military services to accelerate adoption of directed-energy technology. 8VC did not respond to Drop Site's questions about Dodd's involvement with the firm. The Pentagon also did not answer Drop Site's questions about Dodd's relationship with Dioltas and other clients. A spokesperson for the War Department said, "The Department of War maintains a rigorous, multi-layered ethics framework that includes financial disclosure reviews, divestitures where appropriate, and screening to prevent conflicts of interest. Every DOW official, including Hon. Mike Dodd, is in full compliance with all ethical laws and regulations. Any claims otherwise are false." Dioltas, in a response to an inquiry, said only, "We highly encourage you to check the facts." "At the Speed of Business" In his May 2025 , Dodd pledged to resign from Dioltas "upon confirmation" and said that within 90 days of assuming his role at the Pentagon, he would divest his ownership in the company by selling his stake. He also said that his wife's role with the firm "will also end when my interest is sold." Those pledges do not appear to have been upheld. The Senate confirmed Dodd on September 18, 2025. But he did not resign from Dioltas until September 2026, according to Indiana Secretary of State . On the same day that he resigned from Dioltas, the records show, his wife took over as the firm's registered agent and his son Keegan became its manager. Two days after telling Drop Site to "check the facts," Dodd's son replaced his wife as registered agent, according to a federal disclosure filed on November 17. Dodd still owns between $1 million and $5 million in Dioltas, according to his most recent annual financial disclosure, which he signed in May and which a government ethics lawyer formally approved in September. That disclosure also shows that, throughout 2025, he received $170,000 from Dioltas. "There's a general prohibition on using public office for private gain," Virginia Canter, a former government ethics lawyer, told Drop Site. "I don't understand why DoD would allow him, as a Pentagon official, to retain a financial interest in a company whose business involves facilitating relationships between the Pentagon and its clients. It just seems like an obvious conflict of interest if he or his family members continue to profit from that business." Drop Site News is funded by readers. Become a paying subscriber to support this work. While Dodd advised defense startups on how to navigate the Pentagon, he simultaneously held senior government positions at the Defense Innovation Unit, or DIU. Dodd worked for DIU from at least 2022 until September 2025, when he was confirmed as assistant secretary of critical technologies, a position that helps steer the military's defense-industrial policy. The six defense-tech sectors that Dioltas in, including quantum technologies and microelectronics, overlap with sectors that Dodd's Pentagon office manages. If a contractor's work falls outside those sectors, Dioltas the ability to introduce it to "stakeholders defining future needs." "The people who shape requirements and fund programs know us by name because we work alongside them," Dioltas's boasts, one of at least a dozen references on the site to its ability to connect clients with government officials to help them earn contracts. Dioltas says it will stay "behind the scenes, where the work gets done" as it guides clients "through the moments where access means something." Since Dodd's confirmation, Dioltas has made at least a dozen social-media posts promoting his official appearances at industry conferences that Dioltas also attended. It has described these events as to with government leaders, and in one case it urged its followers to register for an event by Dodd's Pentagon office. The event, held in October, introduced the successor to a research contract managed by the Defense Technical Information Center, which reports to Dodd's office. Under the current version of the contract, ManTech, which Dioltas has previously listed as a client, won two awards worth up to around $542 million earlier this year. DTIC did not answer Drop Site's questions about whether Dodd's office was involved. Wes Bryant, an Air Force special operations veteran who served as chief of the Pentagon's recently Civilian Protection Center, told Drop Site that Dioltas was "very clearly, without saying it, selling access directly to him right on their website." Bryant previously worked in business development for defense contractors including L3Harris. A key objective of the work was developing relationships with Pentagon officials. He said that he was required to log each government contact he engaged and rate their value for influencing contract decisions. Someone in Dodd's position would be deemed high value. "Those are the relationships that people out in industry salivate over," Bryant said. Dodd has championed acquisition reform as a primary of accelerating the military's adoption of commercial technology. He has advocated the expansion of a funding arrangement that fast-tracks the contracting process and federal acquisition regulations, known as "Other Transaction Authority" (OTA). As assistant secretary for critical technologies, Dodd works within the Office of Research and Engineering, which supervises department-wide prototyping of technology, much of which runs through OTAs. "If I meet a non-traditional company that I'm interested in, I can get them on contract at the speed of business," Dodd said in an October . William Hartung, an expert on Pentagon budgeting, described OTAs as lucrative long-term commitments with minimal oversight. "Dodd's promotion of OTAs could pad the bottom lines of Dioltas's clients," he told Drop Site. Companies with ties to Dodd have received fast-tracked funding in technology areas he oversees. For example, SkyWater Technology, a Dioltas client and microelectronics manufacturer, received $30.9 million in OTA funding in June. Dodd gave a speech at a the following month and invests up to $15,000 in the firm, according to his disclosures. Allen Control Systems, a startup with no federal contracts in procurement records before Dodd took office, received two prototype OTAs worth at least $6.5 million earlier this year, which funded efforts to adapt its technology for the Army and the Marines. It then won an Army counter-drone contract to $500 million in September, and a few months later, in mid-November, it was selected to join a test program to lead directly to funding. Dodd's office is a partner on this program. Venture capitalists and contractors have pushed to expand the use of OTAs, as they over negotiations and reduce transparency and oversight. The Silicon Valley Defense Group celebrated the Trump administration's embrace of OTAs in its included Dodd's statement to investors and founders that "the Department's checkbook is open" for fast-moving firms. In recent , Dodd has explained that one way he gets firms on contract as fast as possible is by routing them through consortiums, or groups of companies. "That can be literally like same day stuff if we want to get a performer on contract," he told last month. Around half of the Pentagon's is directed to consortiums. Federal records list the consortium as the recipient of a federal contract, and often do not show which individual firms were paid through it. The Government Accountability Office and the War Department's have flagged weak oversight of these middlemen. "A Conflict on Steroids" Dodd worked as an advisor to the National Security Technology Accelerator, or NSTXL, from August 2021 to June 2025. NSTXL is a nonprofit that manages consortia of defense companies and handles in Pentagon contracts, including a Space Force OTA worth up to . NSTXL OTA contracts for Dodd's, including a new related to energy weapons worth up to . Another OTA it manages, which is used across the Pentagon's research and engineering office, has handled more than $3 billion in awards, according to . Dodd's Pentagon microelectronics program, the Microelectronics Commons, is among the projects that run through it. Dodd the Pentagon's leadership keynote at the Microelectronics Commons annual meeting in February, an event organized by NSTXL, where Dioltas said it "engaging with our portfolio companies, industry partners, and Department of War leadership." Drop Site reviewed more than $100 million worth of recent OTAs to NSTXL that do not detail which member firms were paid. NSTXL does not list its members publicly, and according to its , it has no written policy for document retention, whistleblowers, and conflicts of interest. NSTXL reported over $10 million in losses in its two most recent tax filings for and . Over the same period, it transferred over $10 million more than its entire revenue to a for-profit firm owned by its founder. NSTXL reported $66.9 million in revenue over 2023 and 2024--mostly from government fees--but paid its contract consultant Innovas a total of $77.3 million over the same period. Tim Greeff, the founder and president of NSTXL, is also CEO and majority owner of Innovas, according to the filings. Dodd reported $303,000 in income and bonus fees from Innovas in both of his disclosures. NSTXL and Innovas did not respond to Drop Site's inquiries. Hartung called NSTXL's relationship with Dodd "a conflict on steroids," adding that "Congress should force disclosure of companies NSTXL funnels money to and look more closely at Dodd's role in brokering and possibly profiting from these arrangements." | A guest post by| Carolina-based investigative reporter Become a Drop Site News Paid Subscriber Drop Site News is reader-supported. ---
Derek, Adam Schiff here. I want to bring you up to date on the latest threat I received from the Trump Justice Department — the second time in two years Trump’s DOJ has come after me. Last week, I received a threat on Justice Department letterhead from Aaron Reitz, the U.S. Attorney for the Southern District of Texas. **Today, I’m responding.** **[Before I tell you more, will you chip in $10 to show you have my back and support my work in the Senate?](https://act.adamschiff.com/go/8046?t=9&amount=10&refcode=aschiff_email_112526_dojresponse&akid=10959%2E5257348%2EiVaoEr)** | | [DONATE NOW→](https://act.adamschiff.com/go/8046?t=10&amount=10&refcode=aschiff_email_112526_dojresponse&akid=10959%2E5257348%2EiVaoEr)
---
Aaron Reitz threatened me with “legal consequences” if I don’t stop investigating and doing oversight of President Trump and the corruption in his administration.
_So why exactly is he threatening me?_
Because I’ve called for oversight and transparency.
Of the massive contributions to Trump’s ballroom, to find out who’s really behind them and whether there’s some kind of crooked bargain at play.
Of Freedom 250, the organization set up to raise money for the Fourth of July celebration.
Of media payments to Donald Trump after he sued ABC and CBS.
Of law firms that have done work for the president after capitulating to his threats.
Essentially, Reitz has made it clear that DOJ will investigate anyone investigating the president.
Here’s the thing, Derek: I’ve read the Constitution.
I know Congress has both the right and the duty to do oversight. And it is crazy to threaten senators for doing their jobs.
**So today, I'm sending a letter to Aaron Reitz telling him that I won’t stop doing my job.**
I’m calling on him to withdraw this absurd request. We’re going to continue doing the oversight that the American people voted for in overwhelming numbers.

**The State of Play**
The petition is real and checkable. Rep. Sylvia Garcia (D-TX-29) filed Discharge Petition No. 25 on July 20, 2026, to discharge the Rules Committee from consideration of the rule for H.R. 1589, the American Dream and Promise Act of 2025 -- the standard end-run when leadership will not schedule a bill.
The count: 218 signatures needed; 217 have signed -- all 214 Democrats plus three Republicans:
**\- Rep. Maria Elvira Salazar (FL-27)**
**\- Rep. Brian Fitzpatrick (PA-01)**
**\- Rep. Don Bacon (NE-02)**
Garcia's own tally: "We just need 1 more Republican." The chamber's lone independent is also being courted.
Detail most coverage skips: the petition has been stuck at 217 since September 2 -- a three-month freeze with no taker.
The clock: reaching 218 does not force an instant vote. The question waits seven legislative days on the House calendar, and the petition _dies_ at noon on January 3, 2027, when the 119th Congress expires.
The midterms changed everything. On November 3, Democrats won the House (roughly 255-259 seats -- the largest majority in 35 years, with 48 seats changing party) and the Senate. Hakeem Jeffries was formally nominated for speaker 251-11 on November 18 and will be elected January 3 as the first Black speaker in history. Donald Trump still holds the veto pen...

**The State of Play**
The petition is real and checkable. Rep. Sylvia Garcia (D-TX-29) filed Discharge Petition No. 25 on July 20, 2026, to discharge the Rules Committee from consideration of the rule for H.R. 1589, the American Dream and Promise Act of 2025 -- the standard end-run when leadership will not schedule a bill.
The count: 218 signatures needed; 217 have signed -- all 214 Democrats plus three Republicans:
**\- Rep. Maria Elvira Salazar (FL-27)**
**\- Rep. Brian Fitzpatrick (PA-01)**
**\- Rep. Don Bacon (NE-02)**
Garcia's own tally: "We just need 1 more Republican." The chamber's lone independent is also being courted.
Detail most coverage skips: the petition has been stuck at 217 since September 2 -- a three-month freeze with no taker.
The clock: reaching 218 does not force an instant vote. The question waits seven legislative days on the House calendar, and the petition _dies_ at noon on January 3, 2027, when the 119th Congress expires.
The midterms changed everything. On November 3, Democrats won the House (roughly 255-259 seats -- the largest majority in 35 years, with 48 seats changing party) and the Senate. Hakeem Jeffries was formally nominated for speaker 251-11 on November 18 and will be elected January 3 as the first Black speaker in history. Donald Trump still holds the veto pen.
**The Two Vehicles Being Bundled as "Amnesty"**
1\. H.R. 1589 -- American Dream and Promise Act (the discharge target). Conditional permanent resident status for **10 years**, for:
\- People who entered the U.S. as minors (DACA-eligible)
\- TPS and DED holders
\- "Documented Dreamers" (children of long-term visa holders)
It is a decade of provisional status first, not instant green cards. The covered pool is roughly 2-3 million depending on the estimate: about 530,000 active DACA recipients, plus a TPS population that peaked near 1 million before the 2025-26 terminations.
2\. H.R. 11120 -- Protect Our Neighbors Act (the "evaporate" bill). Introduced November 19, 2026 by Rep. Lateefah Simon (D-CA), with Reps. Lofgren, Garamendi and Vargas. It would make **final orders of removal expire 10 years after issuance** (time in the country before the order does not count), for people continuously present who have not been convicted of a crime punishable by more than one year. Judges could renew an expired order only on clear-and-convincing evidence of a justified delay. A separate green-card pathway is created.
The numbers behind the tweets:
| [](https://substack.com/redirect/d0f24fe6-063e-4479-8fd6-a8a06b722cd8?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)|
---|---|---
The "decades old orders would just EVAPORATE", only for the continuously present with clean records, renewable by judges -- and expiration of an order is not itself legal status.
**How We Got Here**
1986 -- IRCA. Reagan signs the last big legalization: ~2.7 million amnestied, in exchange for employer sanctions and border control. The enforcement half never materialized -- worksite enforcement quietly collapsed -- and the unauthorized population roughly tripled over the following two decades.
| [](https://substack.com/redirect/7ccc80f2-b312-44ed-ac5f-b476fafdf105?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)|
---|---|---
1988-1994 -- California. The electoral facts often cited check out: 54 electoral votes in 1988, the last Republican presidential win there. But the flip was multi-causal -- the Cold War aerospace collapse, a doubling Latino electorate, and the Prop 187 backlash -- not the single hand of IRCA. "Reagan's amnesty flipped California" is a defensible parable, not a documented single cause.
2006-07 -- the word is forged. Bush-Kennedy-McCain comprehensive reform dies under a grassroots revolt; "amnesty" becomes the term that breaks GOP coalitions. The restrictionist infrastructure (NumbersUSA, FAIR, CIS) dates from this era -- which is why NumbersUSA is doing the granular petition coverage now.
2013-14 -- the playbook. The Gang of Eight bill passes the Senate 68-32 and dies in Boehner's House without a vote. Two legacies: the Democratic conviction that the committee route can be an ambush, and the discharge-petition instinct now on display.
2019-21 -- the rehearsal. The Dream and Promise Act (as H.R. 6) passes the House twice under Democratic control and dies in the Senate. H.R. 1589 is the third bite.
2024-26 -- the trigger. The border surge makes immigration a top-two voter issue and powers Trump's 2024 win. The administration's enforcement push then runs into a June 2026 Supreme Court decision empowering the administration to dissolve DACA/TPS protections nearly at will -- the ruling that prompted Garcia to file her petition on July 20. Then the midterms: a 48-seat wave on affordability hands Democrats Congress, and Jeffries pledges to move the bill "immediately."
**The Strategic Read**
\- "One signature away" is a targeting operation, not a vote count. Even at 218, the lame-duck House vote is a message vote that dies in the current GOP Senate. The missing name would buy the headline "House protects Dreamers with Republican votes" -- and put a primary target on whoever signs. That is why the three signers are the usual bipartisan-immigration suspects (Salazar wrote the Dignity Act; Fitzpatrick and Bacon hold swing/suburban turf) and why no fourth has moved in three months.
\- The real bill arrives January 3. With a Democratic House and Senate, it passes; Trump's veto is the actual wall. Expect "make him say no" veto-fight framing to be the story of spring 2027.
\- The affordability seam is the GOP's best attack. Jeffries' stated 100-day agenda is cost-of-living and oversight; the wave ran under "Fighting for an Affordable America." The "amnesty first, affordability forgotten" line is a sequencing bet -- watch what bill number the Dream Act gets in January.

body:
These three steps will help you have productive conversations with almost anyone.
#
Hi there,
If you’re anything like us, you’re still riding the high of the blue tsunami earlier this month.
**But if you’re anything like most Americans, you’ll be celebrating Thanksgiving tomorrow amongst conflicted company:** the uncle who supports Donald Trump, the longtime Republican grandparents who are disappointed with the direction of their party, or the cousin who never votes.
While some people dread talking politics at the Thanksgiving table, it’s actually a great opportunity to start a conversation you can continue over the next two years and build the trust needed to win a few hearts and minds.
**Using the Ground Truth program as a guide, these three steps will help you have productive conversations with almost anyone:**
1. **Ask open-ended questions.** Start the conversation by asking someone what matters to them. Are they worried about food quality and outbreaks? Are they thinking about their kids’ safety at school? Do they wonder if the price of gas will ever go down? These are all gateways to deeper conversations about our country.

2. **Use nonjudgmental listening.** No matter what someone shares, the best way to earn their trust is to listen with an open mind. The key here is to listen more than you share and to practice curiosity towards what is being shared with you. "Tell me more about that" is a powerful tool in your toolbox.

3. **Share what matters to you.** Trust is a two-way street. Think about what about our country keeps you up at night, and share that at a level that is most comfortable for you.

If the conversation is going well, don’t be afraid to talk to them about why you vote for Democrats. You might be surprised by what you hear!
Above all else, we hope you have a happy Thanksgiving with the chance to spend time with your loved ones. The Swing Left community worked hard to power Democratic victories this year, and we’re thankful for every member of this team.
Thank you, as always, for doing your part.
— The Swing Left Team
_P.S. We want to hear how your conversations go! You can send us any stories, notes, or thoughts by replying directly to this email._

I’m thankful for the parents who showed up at my patients’ bedsides, worried, and still doing everything they could to give their children a better future. I’m thankful for the teachers who stay late, buy supplies with their own money, and show up for kids who need a steady adult more than they’ll ever know. I’m thankful for every member of our community who stands up when something is wrong, even when it would be easier to stay quiet. **And I’m deeply thankful for this grassroots team.** For every person who volunteered, shared a post, donated whatever they could, or simply believed that South Carolina deserves leadership rooted in compassion and reality, not corruption and political games. Running this campaign while raising three kids wasn’t easy. But what kept me going was knowing how many people want a future where families aren’t crushed by healthcare costs, where gun violence isn’t the leading cause of death for kids, and where women can make their own decisions about their own bodies. That hope — your hope — means everything to me. [If you’re able, and only if it feels right, I would be grateful if you helped keep this movement strong as I prepare to take office. "Starlink-7 over California" by Forest Katsch via Unsplash
Before becoming a young entrepreneur, Élie Cantin-Nantel was a college student and journalist at a Canadian news and commentary outlet. His initial post-college plan? Law school.
"I wanted to become a lawyer, and then I realized I could make as much money as an entrepreneur and not spend $60,000 on a law degree," Élie told me. While covering a Canadian election campaign, he noticed YouTubers independently doing similar work. It was then that he had his epiphany about what his entrepreneurial path could look like. "If they can do it, then maybe I can give it a try."
The Compute Optimist is a reader-supported publication. To receive new posts and support my work, consider becoming a free or paid subscriber.
[Upgrade to paid](https://substack.com/redirect/2/eyJlIjoiaHR0cHM6Ly93d3cudGhlY29tcHV0ZW9wdGltaXN0LmNvbS9zdWJzY3JpYmU_.KwKrpeKGBhUBQ6ggg3bQYJ0pVCn7A11331mNsYnnOgo?&utm_medium=email&utm_source=subscribe-widget-preamble&utm_content=226291423)
Not long after, in his final year before graduating, Élie founded [EMCN Media](https://substack.com/redirect/89755deb-0359-458f-b5ec-9ca6780aeb9c?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg), a Canada-based digital media company that produces video content on Canadian, American, and international political and cultural topics. Today, EMCN is Élie's full-time, YouTube-centric venture, putting out videos he describes as monologues, interviews, or documentaries. As the saying goes, time is money, something Élie quickly learned from a job that often puts him in the air for things like firsthand reporting, filming, and in-person interviews. And when slow and unreliable internet interrupts upload work, costs can start piling up.
Élie is joined by many others, with a 2024 American Express [survey](https://substack.com/redirect/6e77f930-0b63-4221-ab4c-f83e4de1fde1?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg) finding 58 percent of business travelers identifying in-flight Wi-Fi as a "must-have." And for years, the commercial aviation experience has been plagued by inadequate internet connectivity. That may be changing. SpaceX's low-Earth-orbit (LEO) satellite internet service, Starlink, is increasingly offering a home-broadband-like experience in the air, and consumers who have experienced it are reluctant to look back. Commercial airlines, competing for those customers, are racing to integrate LEO satellite internet.
United Airlines, an early Starlink adopter, is offering a window into positive consumer sentiment. In 2026, the airline [reported](https://substack.com/redirect/cc0ef958-4b5f-4824-8c22-eba95f59bda3?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg) its highest Wi-Fi customer satisfaction score since 2023, with Starlink-equipped flights receiving more than _double_ the satisfaction scores of aircraft using traditional Wi-Fi systems. And United is already reaping the benefits, with some customers even shifting airline loyalty after trying it out for the first time. One [customer](https://substack.com/redirect/5db2b5e5-7a74-4e91-afe5-f8b1d3488d52?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg) said, "The experience impressed me enough that I've flown United every trip since."
But for entrepreneurs like Élie, reliable airline internet service is about more than just convenience or entertainment.
Speaking to me virtually from a hotel in Paris, Élie told me about how much his work keeps him at 30,000 feet. In October alone, he took roughly 10 or 12 flights. "I've spent this year basically more than a week on airplanes, cumulatively." And these aren't just quick one- or two-hour flights, with his travels often taking him across countries and continents. An eight-hour flight can mean a missed upload, and in turn, lost revenue.
What if slow and unreliable in-flight internet could be a thing of the past? For Élie, it could mean the end of thousands of dollars in lost revenue in any given month. "A YouTube video, at least on my channel, makes anywhere low end of like $150 to high end of over $2,000," Élie explained, describing unstable in-flight connectivity over long travel periods as "not just an inconvenience," but lost revenue.
"Will, no video today," he'll often have to text his contractor. "Wi-Fi isn't working." As Starlink becomes more advanced and mainstream in commercial air travel, that text message could become a relic.
Starlink's LEO satellite model enables in-flight internet service with lower latency (less lag time) by operating satellites that orbit closer to Earth. This distance matters because of how long it takes a signal to travel, with Starlink's LEO satellites [orbiting](https://substack.com/redirect/a5202cd7-059f-4c93-bf2a-d2befd1f3ed0?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg) at roughly 340 miles above Earth and traditional geostationary (GEO) satellites at roughly 22,236 miles. Moreover, Starlink [allows for](https://substack.com/redirect/2522165b-22c0-432c-949b-781be517cecc?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg) faster service than GEO satellites typically offer in the air today by scaling far more of its LEO satellites (as of writing, there are roughly 11,200 active Starlink satellites [in orbit](https://substack.com/redirect/1f56647b-20d9-4293-b6c2-c645c8343bdd?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)). Each Starlink satellite generally covers a smaller area and fewer people than a GEO satellite. The scale of satellites and how many people each serves matters because it means each user gets a bigger piece of the capacity pie, resulting in less congestion and faster upload and download speeds.
Starlink is demonstrating LEO's advantage in the real world. Ookla, an internet performance measurement company, [sets](https://substack.com/redirect/a73b8db1-792f-42ad-a24c-1be2bfd85a16?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg) download and upload speed thresholds for in-flight connectivity of 25 megabits per second (Mbps) and 3 Mbps, respectively. It considers these thresholds "practical requirements for digital productivity and entertainment," with download speeds above 25 Mbps enabling buffer-free high-definition streaming and upload speeds above 3 Mbps helping facilitate reliable cloud-based work.
In [speed testing](https://substack.com/redirect/a73b8db1-792f-42ad-a24c-1be2bfd85a16?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg) covering the latter half of 2025 measuring in-flight Wi-Fi provider performance, Starlink was found to vastly outperform these thresholds. Its median download and upload speeds were measured at roughly 213 Mbps and 30 Mbps, respectively. Ookla observed: "Starlink was so much faster than its competitors that even its worst performance was better than their typical service." Furthermore, the performance measurement company particularly highlighted the gap in upload speeds. "This lead was even greater when it came to upload speeds; Starlink's bottom 10th percentile (11.73 Mbps) were nearly as fast as the top users on Intelsat's network (13.84 Mbps) and were significantly faster than everyone else."
For reference, _[BroadbandNow](https://substack.com/redirect/5192c200-f671-412d-8560-9259d7e65841?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)_ recommends upload speeds of 10 Mbps for 1080p YouTube uploads and 20 to 30 Mbps for 4K YouTube uploads. Assuming other factors do not stand in the way, Starlink's median speeds in commercial aviation appear to be a game changer for Élie's video uploads, and certainly for basic cloud computing work.
The latency gap is massive, too. Remember, the lower the lag time, the better. Starlink's median multi-server latency was measured at 43 milliseconds (ms), 689 ms faster than the next best competitor's median of 732 ms.
None of this is to say GEO satellite internet is unusable, and Ookla [makes clear](https://substack.com/redirect/a73b8db1-792f-42ad-a24c-1be2bfd85a16?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg) that some GEO satellite internet providers are still providing what it describes as "usable Wi-Fi." And in November 2025, GEO satellite internet provider Viasat [deployed](https://substack.com/redirect/75bd69fb-4f55-4db7-9bd3-60f78a6556b7?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg) a new satellite into orbit designed in part to serve broadband customers.
Nevertheless, usability is a floor expectation, and the service quality gap between LEO- and GEO-based internet providers is enormous. What Starlink is demonstrating is that its satellite constellation's speeds are not only outshining GEO speeds but also competing with home broadband speeds. For context, to receive federal funding under the Broadband Equity, Access, and Deployment (BEAD) Program, a provider must demonstrate it can meet [benchmarks](https://substack.com/redirect/0bdae4d6-4488-4fb3-9136-99d2b3ec6d41?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg) of 100 Mbps download speeds, 20 Mbps upload speeds, and round-trip latency of 100 ms in at least 95 percent of tests. Starlink is not merely usable on commercial flights. At median performance, it is already emerging as a provider that can offer a home-broadband-like experience.
United may be an early adopter of LEO satellite internet, but it is far from alone, with more than 40 global airlines [announcing](https://substack.com/redirect/86872fb1-53cc-47af-86ff-9649a09a6b12?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg) they will integrate Starlink into their flights. And as recently as October, American Airlines [announced](https://substack.com/redirect/3989059a-b6f6-4a2a-9d91-499fc907d4be?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg) it would expand upon its initial Starlink investment, committing to installing Starlink service into "every mainline jet." Meanwhile, at least two airlines have announced [deals](https://substack.com/redirect/1f4b177c-0744-454a-a3cc-c51f647c1db1?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg) with Starlink's emerging competitor, Amazon Leo.
It is worth noting that Amazon Leo has faced some setbacks in the deployment of its planned LEO satellite constellation, and in June, the FCC [waived a rule](https://substack.com/redirect/c3dce4e6-965b-45ee-8351-864339825c93?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg) requiring Amazon to have approximately 1,600 satellites in orbit by this past July as the company fell behind in meeting this deadline. In May, Blue Origin's New Glenn rocket [exploded](https://substack.com/redirect/648de2eb-382d-497c-9c09-2acc55ecf5c5?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg) during a static fire test. And this month, Amazon Leo [lost](https://substack.com/redirect/f986bd45-3ae0-4134-98fd-c9c934a35759?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg) 40 LEO satellites set to be deployed after United Launch Alliance's (ULA) Vulcan rocket failed to deliver them into orbit. Both rockets were grounded as a result.
With Vulcan and New Glenn set to be major launch vehicles for Amazon Leo, the timing of the company's full-scale commercial launch is a bit uncertain. Still, there is reason for optimism.
Just today, Amazon successfully sent 36 new satellites [into orbit](https://substack.com/redirect/2d25d564-8a5a-41cc-916f-988c4b7e7c2c?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg), increasing the number of LEO satellites it has in orbit to [roughly 430](https://substack.com/redirect/70930828-7bee-4bb4-9da1-04a73b16dc29?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg). Further, New Glenn is [slated](https://substack.com/redirect/d75d03d3-75b5-45e6-831c-5f1e5c99439c?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg) to fly again in January 2027, and the company still plans to launch satellite service before the end of 2026. Following the November Vulcan failure, Amazon Leo appears undeterred, with _[Fierce Network](https://substack.com/redirect/03a1c925-9011-4f81-9d3f-b1151c6c759a?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)_ reporting that Amazon says it is "pressing ahead." Fierce says Amazon already has enough satellites in orbit to launch commercial service "across certain latitudes."
While it may be some time before Amazon Leo catches Starlink, it shouldn't be lost that commercial LEO satellite internet remains a novel concept, one largely viewed as unworkable not long ago. Just months after Elon Musk announced his initial plans to build a commercial LEO satellite internet project, in 2015, _Wired_ published an article titled "[Internet by Satellite Is a Space Race With No Winners](https://substack.com/redirect/fca5a85f-b6fe-4db0-a237-d141501b3e15?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)." In 2018, in an _Inverse_ article titled "[Elon Musk's SpaceX Satellite Internet Plan Slammed by Experts](https://substack.com/redirect/d6a1cd4d-4054-4b3e-97a7-786e4a2219ad?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)," one "expert" was quoted on the subject as saying, "Nothing has changed except the level of hysteria and the level of unrealistic expectations."
Even as late as mid-2024, none of the four largest U.S. commercial airlines had announced LEO satellite internet integration. Today, all are joining the LEO buildout. Past performance is not indicative of future results, as the saying goes. And when Starlink was still a concept and emerging, the past performance of other LEO satellite ventures [wasn't great](https://substack.com/redirect/6db128f6-f88b-4453-8088-7f3c96b3958c?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg). Musk pushed forward anyway. Today, Starlink, a primarily privately financed venture, is SpaceX's [profitable](https://substack.com/redirect/02b54162-49a5-4bec-b6fc-5c8ccedca6fe?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg) operation. Amazon Leo may be facing setbacks but should be lauded, like SpaceX, for also risking its own private capital in its efforts to achieve something extraordinary.
A concept seen as science fiction a short time ago is now transforming how we use and access the internet. And Starlink has proven it to be profitable. Its success is a testament to capitalism, risk-taking, and people who dare to try something thought impossible. Once scaled in commercial air travel, LEO satellite internet means better entertainment, yes. But for entrepreneurs like Élie, it can mean building one's dream that day or not.
_Ed Tarnowski is the Founder and Editor of The Compute Optimist and a Resident Fellow, Technology and Innovation at the R Street Institute. All opinions expressed are his own._

name: Pramila Jayapal
subject: Big Money lost on Tuesday
disclaimer_text: Paid for by Pramila for Congress
body:
Politicians shouldn’t be bought. Corporations shouldn’t decide elections.
# [](https://act.pramilaforcongress.com/go/892?refcode=em20261125-6991-footer&t=1&akid=6991%2E420207%2E3iqVej)
**Corporations are not people, Peter. And money is not speech.**
_So why are corporations allowed to spend unlimited amounts of money influencing our elections?_
In 2010, the Supreme Court sided with _Citizens United_ , a right-wing organization, in a decision that opened the floodgates for unlimited corporate spending in our elections.
It’s been destructive for our democracy ever since because corporations can now buy political influence.
Instead of politicians answering to their constituents, they answer to Big Tech, the insurance industry, and Big Pharma. They put their own profits over the people they represent.
**But onthis month, voters made one thing clear: people power is stronger than any GOP warchest bankrolled by billionaires and corporations.**
Trump and his handpicked candidates learned the hard way that money, baseless attacks, and more money cannot cover up a devastatingly high cost of living, reckless illegal wars, gutted healthcare, and an administration that serves itself instead of the people.
Voters showed up to the polls in record numbers and showed Republicans that all the millions of dollars they poured into their races were not enough to drown out the blatant corruption and the deeply unpopular Republican agenda.
**Because money doesn’t vote._People do._**
That’s why I’ll keep fighting against corporate greed and continue to introduce legislation to end _Citizens United_. Now that we’ve taken back the House and Senate, we’re closer than ever to getting dark money out of politics for good.

[**So Peter, if you’re in this fight with me, add your name to help end Citizens United and ensure our representatives only answer to the people they represent.** ](https://act.pramilaforcongress.com/sign/em20261125-citizens-united-petition/?source=em20261125-6991&t=2&akid=6991%2E420207%2E3iqVej)

In solidarity,
Pramila Jayapal

Okay, it's here. The GOP/MAGA/Big Tech/Big Oil "permitting reform" bill to gut our bedrock environmental laws passed the Senate last week, and it has been scheduled for a vote in the House on Monday. If there were ever a time to call or email your Congressperson to express your concern over this, the time is right now. [Here's a tool for doing so.](https://substack.com/redirect/3489fdc9-e7d2-490c-9aee-b0ad53e58b81?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)
I wrote a [general review](https://substack.com/redirect/396be5b4-635e-49f1-a418-78e0aad28525?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg) of this bad bill last week. I wanted to share another piece I wrote for _[Current Affairs](https://substack.com/redirect/34e14cda-dc32-46cc-b805-93bf62f25e59?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)_[ (they're great, check them out here)](https://substack.com/redirect/34e14cda-dc32-46cc-b805-93bf62f25e59?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg) that specifically discusses how the legislation eviscerates the Endangered Species Act. Thanks for taking a look.

Have you ever seen a bald eagle in flight? There's something about it--beyond the unbidden twinge of national pride--that makes for a capital 'E' Experience. My last sighting, this past September, was particularly special, because I was with my five-year-old son. Like so many children, he _loves_ animals, and seeing the creatures he knows from books and stuffies as real breathing beings, alive and in the wild, is just about as good as it gets for him.
We were out kayaking, and my son, ever on the lookout, saw the bird first, a growing black speck against the light blue sky. I figured it was an osprey, which would have been exciting enough. But as it drew closer, and the white head and tail came into focus, we realized this was a full-fledged eagle gliding toward us. It wasn't a particularly dramatic run-in--there was no talon-extended dive to pluck a fish out of the water. And we never got particularly close, though the eagle's route intersected with ours enough to give us some sense of its size, which even from its height was a bit disorienting--a creature of such dimensions really shouldn't be able to move through the air like that, right?
We were on a one-night camping trip that featured plenty of memorable moments--swimming to the big rock in the middle of the pond, roasting marshmallows over the fire, all the usual hits. But the only thing the boy wanted to tell his mom about when we got home was that eagle.
Recently, as I've been drawn into the fight over the seismically far-reaching "permitting reform" package currently working its way through the lame-duck Congress, I have found myself thinking about how easily we might have been consigned to a different timeline, one where we never got to see that eagle, or any of its living kin. It's a timeline where my son might have asked me "What bird is that?" while pointing at a pickup truck decal or fingering the back of a quarter, and I'd have had to answer, "That's a bald eagle. They used to live here in America. But they're gone now."
The point of departure between that timeline and ours is easy to pinpoint: the 1973 passage of the Endangered Species Act (ESA), a capstone accomplishment in the history of conservation that the U.S. Supreme Court later [called](https://substack.com/redirect/9378df3f-017c-47b6-b6bb-4294b035f26a?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg) "the most comprehensive legislation for the preservation of endangered species ever enacted by any nation." The law requires the government to maintain a list of species that are at risk of extinction and take action to protect them, most significantly by prohibiting their "taking"--hunting, trapping, capturing, disturbing--and, at least until very recently, protecting the "critical habitat" necessary for their survival.
The year the ESA was enacted there were only 791 adult nesting pairs of bald eagles in the lower forty-eight states. Thanks to the protections of the ESA, as well as the EPA's banning of DDT, the bald eagle was not only saved from extinction but supported in making a substantial comeback. Today there are an [estimated](https://substack.com/redirect/43f86045-b1a4-4ee2-a259-85fe165abe97?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg) 316,700 bald eagles in the continental U.S., including the one that flew above our kayak several months ago.
In my imagined alternative timeline, where the U.S. Congress and that crazed lefty environmentalist Richard Nixon failed to pass the ESA, it's not just bald eagles we'd have had to describe to our kids like passenger pigeons or dodos. In 1975 there were only [324 nesting pairs ](https://substack.com/redirect/602b248d-3de9-4ec2-a284-7abb5d1575d5?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)of American peregrine falcons in the U.S. Today there are an [estimated](https://substack.com/redirect/5f2a37c5-7a29-4e33-b9ec-ec2892562752?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg) 72,000 individuals. The [American alligator](https://substack.com/redirect/78dbb705-30ea-4804-925a-0a0b9358b741?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg) was similarly saved by the ESA, as were [Florida manatees](https://substack.com/redirect/ae2d6afe-4a62-4b64-bcc6-c6d9a70ce550?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg), [humpback whales](https://substack.com/redirect/6f93f6c8-e0e8-4bc2-a24f-c85743e8bee2?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg), [lower-48 grey wolves](https://substack.com/redirect/e76ef771-6d9a-4871-88a4-3b577180c337?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg), and approximately 750 other animal species. Unlike the bald eagle, many are still severely threatened--for example, there are only 600 California condors remaining on our planet. But that's up from a 1980s-era nadir of 22 individuals, thanks to an ESA-backed [recovery program](https://substack.com/redirect/fc1d0b75-6669-4cb1-8add-b1ef769366a6?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg).
The point is, in an age of planetary arson and callous disregard for the non-human world, the ESA is a triumph of public policy. It's an example of people--politicians, bureaucrats, scientists, lawyers--coming together to protect and save, rather than rapaciously destroy, the remaining wildlife that against all odds has continued making this home of ours magic. It's an achievement--like the defeat of the Nazis in World War II, or the passage of the Civil and Voting Rights Acts--to feel genuine, unvarnished pride in as Americans.
[Upgrade to paid](https://substack..2F-RF39dNoNNjLWKTW-NVnif4p1D4jLpDI7casfbf_E?&utm_medium=email&utm_source=subscribe-widget&utm_content=226565231)
Naturally, then, as with so much that is good and worthy in our country, the ESA has become an obsessive target of corporate and far right interest groups like the Heritage Foundation (the organization behind Project 2025) which has [wanted](https://substack.com/redirect/52b0f759-9919-4631-b5b6-0db54381b6ec?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg) to [overturn](https://substack.com/redirect/44732cc6-4245-434d-8893-fd902afd470a?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg) the [ESA](https://substack.com/redirect/b2ccd4c7-d79b-4be3-bfa7-8ad532220e53?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg) for [decades](https://substack.com/redirect/3a449597-945b-462c-87d4-c1a6985c5071?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg) and prominently called for its [dismantling](https://substack.com/redirect/3b799323-98a4-42d4-9d74-5fa1048b963d?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg) in Project 2025.
While the public strongly approves of the ESA--the law has the support of more than [80 percent of Americans](https://substack.com/redirect/371602d5-1014-46f6-8925-010e773c98d7?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)--these ideological opponents have long bemoaned the red tape and litigation they say it has fostered. Attempts to weaken the ESA have been particularly hot and heavy under Trump, from the delisting of still-threatened species to the administration's utterly devastating [removal](https://substack.com/redirect/fee68d56-dcde-40f7-a95b-4f70fef05a35?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg) of habitat destruction from the regulatory definition of "harm" under the law, a strike at the very heart of the ESA's protective framework. But as battered and bruised as the ESA has become, at the very least the recent changes to it have been administrative actions, reversible after 2028 by a future Democratic administration.
Until now. On November 19, the Senate voted 62-33 for the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA), with 15 Democrats joining nearly the entire GOP caucus in passing this top legislative priority of [Donald Trump](https://substack.com/redirect/4626b96c-e088-4418-8a78-80bfdd755979?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg), [Steven Miller](https://substack.com/redirect/3062b075-9992-48ea-a3a6-cd382fe5188f?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg), [Big Oil](https://substack.com/redirect/70da2a64-937a-43c4-a7be-245c4b00eb2a?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg), and [Big Tech](https://substack.com/redirect/7fd493d0-bd91-452c-b54a-719cd7f152fc?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg).
BAAJA, which was negotiated in secret, is being rammed through without any hearings or usual procedure in the final days of the GOP's legislative majority, just weeks before Democrats take control of Congress. The 500-page package, large portions of which were [taken](https://substack.com/redirect/1904064b-f50f-4722-a091-f4bda3874678?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg) straight out of Project 2025, does a lot of bad stuff--I wrote a broader overview of the bill for _[The New Republic](https://substack.com/redirect/74c643f4-b718-478e-b9f8-e3315ebae7be?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)_. But some of its most egregious assaults are directed at the ESA.
For example, BAAJA allows for states to take over the ESA's core protective mechanism, endangered species reviews, from the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service. These reviews, called consultations, evaluate projects to ensure they won't threaten the survival of any listed species, and require reasonable measures to mitigate such risks if they exist. To be clear, this process is not a critical obstacle to clean energy development, as [BAAJA advocates](https://substack.com/redirect/a17226b7-fe86-4833-a2fe-fca66e1f5279?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg) have claimed. A [peer-reviewed study](https://substack.com/redirect/0c74c0aa-fb1f-471d-acd7-0b2bdef4ac8c?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg) of 88,290 ESA-required consultations found that not a single project was ultimately stopped by these reviews, and only a few were significantly delayed. Indeed, the study found that formal consultations took on average just two months to complete, while informal consultations, which constitute 90 percent of these reviews, took only two weeks, far faster than one could expect under-funded state agencies to manage. Of course, it doesn't in any way help interstate developers to move from a uniform system to a permitting patchwork like this--but that's not the point.
The real rationale for devolving this core ESA function is that many states are explicitly hostile to the ESA and have actively sought to dismantle federal endangered species protections. Even states that are not ideologically hostile will often have financial incentives to facilitate harmful projects; for example, half the money from federal oil and gas lease sales goes to states. And BAAJA contains no safety-valve provision for federal oversight in the case of a misguided state consultation, meaning that in these instances, ESA delegation amounts to a functional repeal of the law's core protections.
And that's just one of a host of assaults on the ESA in this "permitting reform" bill. BAAJA redefines the scientific standard by which agencies must act to protect endangered animals, restricting precautionary action and likely condemning many wildlife populations to destruction before the new benchmarks for establishing scientific certainty could possibly be met. The bill exempts many highway projects from the ESA altogether, despite the fact that roads can obliterate habitat and vehicle strikes are a leading cause of death for many endangered species. And it opens public lands for mining companies to dump waste and otherwise foul critical habitats.
Arguably most insidious of all, BAAJA severely restricts the ability of communities and conservation groups from bringing ESA challenges--the core mechanism for citizen enforcement of the law--by directing all such cases to the U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit and cutting the amount of time available to bring such challenges by more than an order of magnitude. This can sound wonky or abstract, but the practical effect of these measures is to bar local community groups--which are unlikely to have fast and easy access to the legal resources necessary to pursue complex federal litigation--from challenging unlawful decisions in time. The far right has long wanted to make the ESA unenforceable. By shutting down access to the courts, BAAJA effectively does so in many--perhaps most--contexts.
The end result of all this is obvious and incontrovertible: More wildlife will be lost. More animals will be endangered. More species will become ecologically extinct. This harm is irreversible. Each time we lose a species, we lose an irreplaceable building block of a healthy ecosystem. Our world unravels a bit more, and we're left with a landscape, and a web of life, that is darker, uglier, and frailer than the one that preceded it.
This is not a new dynamic, of course. The story of America has in many ways been a story of ecological decimation--the slaughter of beavers for hats, whales for oil, wolves for livestock, passenger pigeons for meat, bison for sport; the bulldozing away of forests, the monocropping away of prairies, the paving away of wetlands. We had already lost so much of this country's magic long before any of us were born; as Henry David Thoreau recorded in his journal back in 1856, "I take infinite pains to know all the phenomena of the spring, for instance, thinking that I have here the entire poem, and then, to my chagrin, I hear that it is but an imperfect copy that I possess and have read, that my ancestors have torn out many of the first leaves and grandest passages, and mutilated it in many places."
This ignoble history makes it even more remarkable, then, that environmental destruction has _not_ just been a one-way ratchet in our country--that in the 1970s Americans chose to change course. In Langston Hughes' [timbre](https://substack.com/redirect/f80b1c52-8317-4dc5-be97-1dd5d68f7c10?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg), we, the people, took action to redeem the plants, the rivers, the mountains, and the endless plain. And in the years since we have made real progress towards conserving these great green states of ours, thanks in large part to the tireless work of activists, scientists, and, yes, bureaucrats and environmental attorneys--the premier villains of every [abundist](https://substack.com/redirect/476cb557-ff9b-4c0d-bc84-36d62fe3eed0?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg) tale spit out over the last two years by the (often Big Tech-backed) think tanks that have worked so hard to create a permission structure for Democrats to jilt many of their core constituencies by supporting BAAJA.
In his 1856 journal entry, Thoreau concluded his musings with these lines: "I should not like to think that some demigod had come before me and picked out some of the best of the stars. I wish to know an entire heaven and an entire earth." My son, like Thoreau, and like every other animal-loving child in our country, deserves to know an entire earth. For 15 Democrats in the Senate, and some as-yet-unspecified number in the House, to join this fascist administration's efforts to dismantle our strongest bulwark against the avarice of corporate interests that would, if allowed, pick out not just the best of the stars, but all of the stars--it is simply unconscionable.

I want to give you a picture of what's really happening right now -- not the polished version, but what it actually looks like on the ground.

Inside our office, tables are covered in supplies and open boxes. Coworkers are coming together, packing materials, sealing kits, and sending them out the door as fast as possible.
---

---
_Above: Activism kits bound for new chapters being packed with Constitutions, chapter handbooks, American flags, and more at TPUSA HQ in Arizona_
---
These boxes aren't sitting around waiting for someone to need them.

They're already claimed. And we don't have extras.

By the time one batch goes out, more requests come in.

Different schools, different students, same situation -- they want to start something, and they're asking us to help them do it.

That's where things stand right now.

We have more students stepping up than we can fully support at the moment.

And I don't say that lightly.

Because for years, the challenge wasn't getting students the tools -- it was getting them to speak up at all. Most kept their heads down.

The Left has spent years trying to convince this generation to sit down, stay quiet, and be ashamed of their country and everything that makes it great.

And for a long time, it worked. But that's all changing.

Now, we're seeing students stand up and push back.

**We saw it clearly at Wheeling High School in the Chicago suburbs -- Charlie's alma mater. **

For the first time, students there launched a Club America chapter. It took months to get approved, but a chapter is finally there.

And now, students are standing outside with signs about free markets and freedom -- not because it's easy, but because they've decided it matters more than staying quiet.
---

---
That's not something you can just manufacture. But it is something you can support when it happens.

And it's not isolated growth anymore.

**We 're now working with more than 1,450 college chapters and over 3,400 high school chapters across the country. That's real scale. **

But if you zoom out, there are roughly 27,000 high schools in America.

That means tens of thousands of campuses where the Left still dominates the conversation...

And where students are waiting for someone to help them stand up and speak.

So as much as this has grown, we're still in the early innings of what Charlie actually set out to build.

What's different now is the pace.

**Many states are moving to bring Club America chapters to every high school statewide, including: **

✅ Arkansas
✅ Florida
✅ Idaho
✅ Indiana
✅ Montana
✅ Nebraska
✅ Oklahoma
✅ South Carolina
✅ Texas
✅ Tennessee

That brings us to ten states now taking this seriously -- not just talk, but action.

That kind of expansion doesn't happen slowly.

It stacks quickly -- and it creates pressure behind the scenes to keep up.

Because every new chapter, every new student leader, every new school means more materials, more support, more follow-through.

And right now, that's where we're stretched.

We're not lacking interest or momentum.

We're working to keep up with both.

_So here 's how you can help... _

Right now, there are students ready to step up -- they just need the tools to do it.

**An activism kit puts everything they need directly into their hands: **

✅ Constitutions.
✅ Chapter guides.
✅ Flags.
✅ Materials to organize and lead.

It turns a student who wants to speak up... _into one who actually does. _

And you'll make it possible for us to keep saying yes when a student reaches out and says, "I want to start something here."

body:
I’m incredibly grateful for your support. | | [](https://click.ngpvan.com/k/144064270/662280401/22799430?refcode=E32543-20261125-Thanksgiving&nvep=ew0KICAiVGVuYW50VXJpIjogIm5ncHZhbjovL3Zhbi9OR1AvTkdQMjQvMS8xMDMxMTgiLA0KICAiRGlzdHJpYnV0aW9uVW5pcXVlSWQiOiAiNDNlMzM1NmEtMTdlOS1mMTExLTkxZjMtMDAwZDNhNTMzMTliIiwNCiAgIkVtYWlsQWRkcmVzcyI6ICJkcHdpbGxpczY3QGdtYWlsLmNvbSINCn0%3D&hmac=50egaHfLz6Rwr9GmiTzHkZ4MFysOq5Fp0K1cCoE4j1I=&emci=2304a41d-49e8-f111-91f3-000d3a533978&emdi=43e3356a-17e9-f111-91f3-000d3a53319b&ceid=6455652) Hey Peter, Before you log off for Thanksgiving, I wanted to share a quick note about what I’m thankful for this year. First, I’m thankful to my wife Pam and my daughters Lillian and Karina for their unconditional love and support — even on the hard days. Second, I’m deeply grateful to every one of you who helped power our campaign to victory and take back the House this year. name: Jim Schultz
subject: Klobuchar said she’d be a pro-growth governor. Now it’s time to prove it.
body:
That means not giving in to everything the soon-to-be DFL-controlled Legislature wants.

| | | | | | | [View this email in your browser](https://mailchi.mp/5f63aac3ab0d/the-briefing-from-mpbc-13064072?e=baf210d431)
---
| | | | |
---
| |
Amy Klobuchar won the governorship of Minnesota after campaigning on an audit of state government, no new taxes, less red tape and an agenda for economic growth. At times, she sounded a little like a Republican. That was encouraging.
But Tim Walz made similar promises eight years ago. Today, Minnesota ranks 49th in per capita GDP growth and 46th in wage growth this decade. We cannot afford another eight years of economic stagnation.
Klobuchar's first test will be whether she has the political courage to say no to her own party. That means vetoing new taxes, rejecting punitive mandates on employers and resisting the demands of the DFL's increasingly ideological left.
But preventing bad policy is not the same as delivering good policy.
Minnesota needs serious tax relief, meaningful permitting reform, an overhaul of the new Paid Family and Medical Leave program and a fundamental change in the culture of state government. Our state agencies have become remarkably adept at finding reasons why things cannot be done. We need a government that helps Minnesotans build, invest and create jobs.
Republicans, too, have an obligation to put forward a serious and compelling vision for Minnesota's future. And the business community should resist the temptation to celebrate incremental improvements after eight years of extraordinarily poor governance.
**Being better than Tim Walz is a low bar. Minnesota needs fundamental change, not a more competent manager of the status quo.**
Klobuchar's campaign rhetoric suggests she understands some of what needs to change. Now we'll see whether she has the courage to deliver.
That is the argument I made in the _Star Tribune_ , and I hope you'll read it.
[**Read the full editorial here.**](https://us.list-manage.com/yHh3NtxvmGA?e=baf210d431&c2id=93c61d534406ea5269257c101c1d1f83)

clean_body: That means not giving in to everything the soon-to-be DFL-controlled Legislature wants. | | | | | | | | | | | | | | Amy Klobuchar won the governorship of Minnesota after campaigning on an audit of state government, no new taxes, less red tape and an agenda for economic growth. At times, she sounded a little like a Republican. That was encouraging. But Tim Walz made similar promises eight years ago. Today, Minnesota ranks 49th in per capita GDP growth and 46th in wage growth this decade. We cannot afford another eight years of economic stagnation. Klobuchar's first test will be whether she has the political courage to say no to her own party. That means vetoing new taxes, rejecting punitive mandates on employers and resisting the demands of the DFL's increasingly ideological left. But preventing bad policy is not the same as delivering good policy. Minnesota needs serious tax relief, meaningful permitting reform, an overhaul of the new Paid Family and Medical Leave program and a fundamental change in the culture of state government. Our state agencies have become remarkably adept at finding reasons why things cannot be done. We need a government that helps Minnesotans build, invest and create jobs. Republicans, too, have an obligation to put forward a serious and compelling vision for Minnesota's future. And the business community should resist the temptation to celebrate incremental improvements after eight years of extraordinarily poor governance. Being better than Tim Walz is a low bar. Minnesota needs fundamental change, not a more competent manager of the status quo. Klobuchar's campaign rhetoric suggests she understands some of what needs to change. Now we'll see whether she has the courage to deliver. That is the argument I made in the Star Tribune , and I hope you'll read it. Here’s what I’m thankful for this year
|
[](https://click.ngpvan.com/k/144064678/662281597/2103691301?refcode=ODP_ATA_EM_NF_Thanksgiving_261125_T3_1&nvep=ew0KICAiVGVuYW50VXJpIjogIm5ncHZhbjovL3Zhbi9OR1AvTkdQMjEvMS84OTI0NyIsDQogICJEaXN0cmlidXRpb25VbmlxdWVJZCI6ICJlY2MxZDY1MS0xYmU5LWYxMTEtOTFmMy0wMDBkM2E1MzMxOWIiLA0KICAiRW1haWxBZGRyZXNzIjogImRwd2lsbGlzNjdAZ21haWwuY29tIg0KfQ%3D%3D&hmac=nUA_PhSkXuxifbyj3moW16y5KDhugMCnjNvnr-45LmQ=) Team,

Every Thanksgiving, my family goes around the table and says what we're thankful for. This year, I've known my answer for weeks: It's the people who stood up for Ohio, when it would have been easier to sit it out.

So before the turkey and the football, I want to take a moment to say thank you.

**I'm thankful for our candidates.** Senator-Elect Sherrod Brown, Governor-Elect Amy Acton, and Democrats up and down the ballot who put their names forward and put in the work. They showed up in every corner of Ohio, and they made the case for working families everywhere they went.

**I'm thankful for our volunteers.** From knocking doors to making phone calls to having conversations with their friends and family, and from Toledo to Portsmouth, Youngstown to Cincinnati, Ohioans gave up their weekend mornings and their evenings alike to talk with their neighbors about what's at stake for Ohio.

**I'm thankful for our grassroots supporters.** Our opponents had dark money and corporate special interests. We had you, and it made all the difference. When folks chip in $10 or $20 at a time, it adds up, and this year it added up to something real – something that beat out the millions of dollars that Republicans’ allies pitched in to try to buy these races.

**And I'm thankful for every Ohio voter who showed up.** That includes the folks who double-checked their registration after Frank LaRose's voter purges and made sure their voices were heard.

Here's what all of that made possible:

Sherrod Brown is headed back to the U.S. Senate to keep fighting for Ohio workers, protect pensions, and lower prescription drug costs. And Dr. Amy Acton, a doctor who knows firsthand what it's like to struggle, will be Ohio's next Governor.

That means a Governor who will stand up for Ohio families. It means a Senator who will keep holding Wall Street and Big Pharma accountable. And it means real progress for Ohio.

We broke the Republican supermajority in the state House, and we flipped multiple U.S. House seats. Democrats won the largest majority in the House this century.

The work isn't over. It never is. But that's a conversation for another day.

Today, I just want to say thank you. From my family to yours, happy Thanksgiving.

With gratitude,

Kathleen Clyde
Chair, Ohio Democratic Party

[_**P.S. If you're in a position to give this holiday season, will you chip in $10 to help us start building for the next fight? We’ll hold on to these gains by investing in organizing now, not waiting for the next Election Day. | | As we head into Thanksgiving, I want to take a moment to wish you and your loved ones a warm and joyful holiday. This has been a year when it's been easy to feel the weight of everything. A president who treats the rule of law like an obstacle, billionaires and corporate interests trying to rig the system, and daily reminders that the alarm bells I keep ringing over the threat to our democratic republic are not overblown. But when I sit down and think about what I'm grateful for, the answer is the people who refuse to give up. I'm grateful for the organizers, volunteers, and neighbors who knocked doors, made calls, and showed up at town halls this year. I'm grateful for the people who stood up for those who couldn't stand up for themselves. And I'm grateful that, even when it's hard, so many of you keep pushing for justice, equality, and a democracy that works for everyone, not because it's easy, but because you know it matters. That is what has always made this work possible. It's ordinary people deciding that our democracy is worth protecting. I'm thankful for you. Your commitment, your engagement, and your hope for a better tomorrow keep me going. Wherever you are, and however you celebrate this week, I hope you find connection, comfort, and a moment of peace with the people you love. Wishing you a very Happy Thanksgiving. clean_body: | | | | As we head into Thanksgiving, I want to take a moment to wish you and your loved ones a warm and joyful holiday. This has been a year when it's been easy to feel the weight of everything. A president who treats the rule of law like an obstacle, billionaires and corporate interests trying to rig the system, and daily reminders that the alarm bells I keep ringing over the threat to our democratic republic are not overblown. But when I sit down and think about what I'm grateful for, the answer is the people who refuse to give up. I'm grateful for the organizers, volunteers, and neighbors who knocked doors, made calls, and showed up at town halls this year. I'm grateful for the people who stood up for those who couldn't stand up for themselves. And I'm grateful that, even when it's hard, so many of you keep pushing for justice, equality, and a democracy that works for everyone, not because it's easy, but because you know it matters. That is what has always made this work possible. It's ordinary people deciding that our democracy is worth protecting. I'm thankful for you. Your commitment, your engagement, and your hope for a better tomorrow keep me going. Wherever you are, and however you celebrate this week, I hope you find connection, comfort, and a moment of peace with the people you love. Wishing you a very Happy Thanksgiving. Onward! Good evening Peter, I hope that you’re about to start a wonderful holiday season surrounded by friends and family. As I spend quality time with my family and loved ones, I can’t help but reflect on how grateful I am for the outpouring of support from you and throughout this community to re-elect me to represent Illinois’ 17th District. And I'm grateful for my first opportunity to work in the majority in Congress, where I know we can check the worst of this administration and deliver necessary relief for so many of us. For those opportunities, I thank each of you. And I hope you have similar things to keep you warm heading into these colder months. I know that for me, I’m not really in the holiday spirit until my partner Shawn whips up his pumpkins bars! And as a small token of gratitude, I want to share my favorite recipe with you, in case you’d like to try it yourself: Now if you’re like me, you probably can’t read that! And that’s because this is a family recipe, and the bakers know exactly what they’re doing. You can find the recipe below in much easier writing to read. Thank you again for being part of this movement. **Pumpkin Bars**
* 1 1⁄2 sticks of unsalted butter (softened)
* 1 15oz can of pumpkin
* 4 eggs
* 2 cups of sugar
* 2 cups of flour
* 2 tsp baking soda
* 1⁄2 tsp salt
* 2 tsp cinnamon
* 1 tsp nutmeg
* 1⁄2 tsp ground clove

1. Preheat oven to 350 degrees
2. Cream butter and sugar till fluffy
3. Mix in eggs one at a time
4. Add can of pumpkin
5. Sift dry ingredients and add to wet ingredients
6. Mix till well combined
7. Bake in 9X13 Pyrex for 25 to 30 minutes or in muffin cups for 20 to 25 minutes

*if using a metal pan butter bottom and sides
**Cream Cheese Frosting**
* 1 stick of unsalted butter (softened)
* 1 8oz package of cream cheese (softened)
* 1 tsp vanilla extract
* 1 tsp almond extract
* 4 cups of powdered sugar sifted

1. Cream the butter, sugar, vanilla extract, and almond extract till light and fluffy
2. Add cream cheese till well incorporated and smooth

Peter, say all you want about pie, I’m not afraid to admit that my favorite Thanksgiving food is actually the cinnamon pull-aparts I make every year. My great-aunt Jessie taught me how to make them. There’s nothing better than enjoying a warm, buttery cinnamon roll (among other dishes!) together while we go around the table and share what each of us is grateful for — another of my favorite Thanksgiving traditions. This year there is _so much_ to be thankful for, coming off incredible November elections and looking ahead to the progress I know we can make together next year and beyond. And having spent many holidays over the years working at the hospital or on call, I never take for granted the opportunity to be with John and our kids on Thanksgiving. From my fellow healthcare providers to service industry professionals to first responders to military service members, there are many Americans who will spend Thanksgiving keeping the rest of us safe, healthy, and fed. To everyone working or serving away from loved ones this holiday — I see you, and I am so thankful for all you do. I hope that no matter how you’re spending tomorrow, you get a moment to connect with someone you love. (And before we sign off for the holiday, I have to know: What’s your controversial favorite Thanksgiving food?! Reply and let me know — bonus points if you share the recipe!)From my family to yours, wishing you a happy and healthy Thanksgiving.Kelly

Congresswoman Kelly Morrison
Minnesota’s 3rd DistrictP.S. Once you try these, you may never go back to pie! Here’s the recipe:_Jessie’s Cinnamon Pull-Aparts_
1\. Thaw one loaf frozen bread dough just until you can slice it.
2\. Cut into 1⁄2” slices, then each into 4 parts.
3\. Dip each piece in melted butter (1⁄2-3⁄4 cup), then in cinnamon sugar (1⁄2-3⁄4 cup).
4\. Place pieces in greased bread pan. Let rise in a warm place until just the size of ready-to-bake loaf of bread.
5\. Bake at 350 degrees, 30-40 minutes.
